title: Approaching the Fundamental Limit of Single-Shot Qubit Frequency Tracking with an Adiabatic Tangentially-Modulated Pulse
authors: Itamar Oren, Luke I. Dyer, Gerardo A. Paz-Silva, Chih Hwan Yang
abstract: Understanding and mitigating noise in two level quantum systems is essential for achieving high fidelity qubit control. Conventional frequency tracking techniques, such as Ramsey interferometry, are fundamentally limited by trade offs between sensitivity, bandwidth, and dynamic range. Here we introduce the adiabatic tangentially-modulated (ATM) pulse, a pulse derived from quantum adiabatic theory that maps qubit detuning onto a sigmoidal, near-binary response. Using numerical simulations supported by analytical modelling, we show that pulse sensitivity and detuning range can be independently engineered through simple design parameters. We derive scaling relations governing these quantities and demonstrate their agreement with simulation. A single shot ATM measurement achieves sensitivity comparable to that obtained from multi-shot Ramsey averaging, enabling tracking of substantially higher frequency noise components with a lower closed-loop white-noise floor. In addition, this pulse exhibits strong robustness to amplitude fluctuations compared with binary response pulses derived from the Shinnar-Le Roux formalism. Together, these properties establish the ATM pulse as a promising approach for robust qubit frequency tracking.
summary: The paper introduces the Adiabatic Tangentially-Modulated (ATM) pulse as an advanced technique for single-shot qubit frequency tracking, overcoming limitations found in standard methods like Ramsey interferometry. By leveraging quantum adiabatic theory, the ATM pulse creates a highly sensitive, sigmoidal response that allows precise measurement of detuning with low noise. This makes it a promising tool for robust, real-time stabilization of qubits against environmental noise.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a single-shot, high-fidelity method for tracking frequency noise in two-level quantum systems that overcomes the fundamental trade-offs inherent in conventional measurement techniques like Ramsey interferometry.
main_result: The proposed Adiabatic Tangentially-Modulated (ATM) pulse achieves sensitivity comparable to multi-shot averaging while maintaining a lower closed-loop white-noise floor and exhibiting superior robustness against amplitude fluctuations compared to existing protocols.
method: The authors derived the ATM pulse using quantum adiabatic theory, designing its time evolution ($\Omega(t)$ and $\omega_D(t)$) such that it maps continuous detuning values onto a highly selective, near-binary response.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a two-level quantum system (qubit), whose dynamics are governed by a time-dependent Hamiltonian in the rotating frame. The protocol involves applying the specially shaped ATM pulse sequence to probe the qubit's detuning ($\Delta$).
key_observables: Detuning-dependent transition probability $P(\Delta)$, sensitivity ($S$), closed-loop noise floor ($P_{	ext{floor}, N}$), and operational detuning range ($\Delta_{	ext{range}}$).
important_parameters: Pulse parameters include rise time ($	au_r$), constant time ($	au_c$), fall time ($	au_f$), and the final gradient $\dot{\Omega}(	au_T)$. Sensitivity scales inversely with the square root of the pulse's rate of change.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the adiabatic condition can be maintained during most of the protocol while allowing controlled non-adiabatic transitions at specific points to achieve the desired readout contrast.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temporal profiles of amplitude and frequency modulation for the ATM pulse, show the geometric evolution on the Bloch sphere corresponding to different detuning regimes, and compare the noise power spectral density (PSD) between ATM and Ramsey tracking methods.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem limitations with conventional techniques, introduces the ATM pulse derived from adiabatic theory, details its mathematical formulation and physical interpretation via Bloch sphere evolution, presents quantitative comparisons of sensitivity and noise floors against Ramsey methods, and concludes by summarizing the practical advantages for real-time stabilization.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, theoretically grounded protocol for improving quantum measurement fidelity in noisy environments. The ability to engineer sensitivity and bandwidth independently is highly valuable for experimentalists working on solid-state qubits where noise mitigation is paramount.
